video.title: Parsons problems: Put the lines in order
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.narration: My Form Three spent a whole lesson typing a ten-line program, and most of them never got it to run. They were stuck on spelling and brackets, not on the idea. So I gave them the lines already written, cut into strips.
Today: Parsons problems, and how to make good ones.

A Parsons problem gives pupils the lines of a working program, mixed up. They put them in the right order, and in Python, indent them too. They’re named after Dale Parsons, who described them in two thousand and six.

Here is the answer. The total starts at zero, then the loop, then the line inside it, indented, then the print after the loop. To solve it, pupils must understand what each line does and where it belongs.

Why do they work? Pupils focus on the logic, not on typing. They can’t make spelling mistakes. A study in two thousand and seventeen found that Parsons problems took less time than writing the same code, with the same learning.

You can add a distractor: a line that looks right but doesn’t belong. Make it the mistake pupils really make, like one equals sign in an if, or a range that stops one too early. Spotting it teaches more than another correct line.
Quick check! Your Parsons problem prints a pass message when mark is at least fifty. Which distractor teaches the most?
The single equals sign. A distractor nobody would choose teaches nothing. A real misconception makes pupils stop and think: which one compares? Collect distractors from your pupils’ own mistakes.

Parsons problems need no device at all. Print the lines on paper, cut them into strips, and put each set in an envelope. Pairs arrange the strips on the desk. Darsi’s printed worksheets have them ready, with boxes to number.

To design one, start from a short program that works, four to eight lines. Check that only one order is right: two lines that could swap make an unfair question. Add one or two distractors, and decide whether pupils must indent.

In the app, open Sorting race and watch bubble sort swap neighbours, pass after pass. Then, in this lesson, rebuild its swap step as a Parsons problem. Seeing the algorithm first makes the lines make sense.
Your turn. A Parsons problem has two lines, name equals Amina and age equals twelve, that could go in either order. Is it a fair question?

scenes.on_screen_text: Order · logic · real distractors · one order
scenes.narration: Not fair. Remember: a Parsons problem orders the lines of a working program. It focuses pupils on the logic, and takes less time than writing. Use real mistakes as distractors, one right order, and paper strips.
Try it in class tomorrow: make a Parsons set. Take a program from your last lesson, print it, cut it into strips, and add one distractor from a real mistake. Pairs race to put it in order.

checkpoints.prompt: The program prints a pass message when mark >= 50. Which distractor teaches the most?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — it’s the mistake pupils really make, so spotting it teaches the difference between = and ==.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a distractor nobody would choose teaches nothing. Use a real misconception, like one equals sign.

checkpoints.prompt: Two lines in a Parsons problem could go in either order. Is it fair?

options.text: No: only one order is marked right

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a pupil could give a right program and be marked wrong. Make each line depend on the one before.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — only one order is marked right, so a correct program could fail. Remove the swap.
